jon-lord.title: Jon Lord
jon-lord.description:
The idea to create this mini-sculpture in Uzhhorod arose in mid-2012, following the death of the legendary composer and founder of the band “Deep Purple,” Jon Lord. The project’s organizers initially began raising funds for the figurine at the “Pid Zamkom” coffee shop, and later at other establishments as well. Beer cans were placed on the bar counters so that anyone could drop coins into them, which would later be used as material to cast the figure of the rock legend. However, after some time, it was decided to change tactics, as the project’s organizers found Czech, Soviet, and even a few Egyptian pounds mixed in with the Ukrainian coins. As a result, they collected about six hundred hryvnias weighing 16 kilograms.

The project organizers, together with the sculptor, decided to depict John Lord with long hair and in the fashionable style of the time—with a cigarette, headphones, and ultra-trendy flared pants. The placement of the statue carries several interesting interpretations. Some point to the cigarette in his hand and say that John Lord is sitting on the banks of the Uzh River, gazing at the water over which a faint mist is slowly spreading, all to the tune of his band Deep Purple’s song “Smoke on the Water.” Others, however, claim that the rock musician’s statue has its back turned toward Korzo Street because, during a previous visit here, John expressed dissatisfaction with the city’s architectural ensemble.

paradjanov.title: Serhii Parajanov
paradjanov.description:
The Serhii Parajanov mini-statue is located near the drama theater in Uzhhorod and is dedicated to the 100th anniversary of the famous director's birth. Next to the mini-statue stands a monument honoring the memory of those who perished in the Armenian Genocide.

Sergei Parajanov is best known for his film adaptation of Mykhailo Kotsyubynsky’s novella *Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors*, which ranks first on the list of the best Ukrainian films. But few people know that Parajanov visited the city of Uzhhorod, and that he co-wrote the screenplay for the film with Ivan Chendey—a renowned Ukrainian writer and screenwriter who spent most of his life in Uzhhorod.

The Serhii Parajanov mini-sculpture depicts a granite stone—symbolizing the artist’s resilience in the face of the Soviet regime—a film reel engraved with the letter “C” (the letter “C” in the Latin alphabet represents the number 100), and Sergei Parajanov holding a pomegranate (a reference to the film “The Color of Pomegranates”). The mini-sculpture was created by Roman Murlik.

bercheni-chaki.title: Miklós Bercsényi and Kristina Csáky
bercheni-chaki.description: This romantic mini-sculpture in Uzhhorod depicts two lovers just moments before a passionate kiss. The pair of figures is dedicated to the memory of a great love that blossomed within the walls of Uzhhorod Castle. The man on the left is Count Miklós Bercsényi, leader of the Hungarian people’s national liberation war. At a young age, he inherited Uzhhorod Castle following the deaths of the first wife and the last male heir of the Druget family. At the age of 22, he became a widower with three children. Some time later, fate brought Miklós Bercsényi and Kristina Csáky together, and they married. At the time they met, Kristina was a widow. Despite the significant age difference—Miklós was nearly half her age—their family was filled with peace and love. Kristina Csáky came from a wealthy family and was a true beauty. Under the couple’s rule, Uzhhorod became a center of cultural and political life. Unfortunately, as in every romantic story, a series of tragic events soon befell the lovers, forcing the couple to flee the castle. In 1710, following the suppression of the uprising, Miklós Bercsényi was declared a traitor, forcing the couple to leave the territory of present-day Transcarpathia. They fled abroad to what is now Turkey, where they found their final resting place after their voluntary exile. You’ll find Uzhhorod’s only paired mini-sculpture at the beginning of the Orthodox Embankment.
